Cut a wide table into column blocks

Source: R/table_plan.R
plan_paginate_cols.Rd

plan_paginate_cols() is the column axis of pagination: a table too wide for one page is cut into blocks of columns, each block a page that repeats the row headings. Say where to cut one way — before named columns (at), into given blocks or by a key in the column names (cut_by), or every so many columns (every, counted when the table exists, so a study with more visits needs nothing rewritten). With order it also says how the three axes nest: this one, the row axis (plan_paginate_rows()) and the group axis (plan_paginate_group()).

Usage

plan_paginate_cols(
  .plan,
  at = NULL,
  cut_by = NULL,
  every = NULL,
  keep = NULL,
  col_header = NULL,
  fit = NULL,
  allow_span_break = NULL,
  order = NULL
)

Arguments

.plan

A table_plan().

at

The columns to cut before, as names or positions, paginate_cols()'s at: at = c(4, 6) makes blocks 1:3, 4:5 and 6: the last.

cut_by

Where to cut other than by position, one of:

a list of column blocks

list(2:3, 4:5).

a separator

one string found in the column names: with "____", "Placebo____Day 1" keys on "Placebo", and each run of one key is a block.

one key per column

a vector as long as the columns; each run of one key is a block.

every

Cut a block every this many columns, counting only the ones a block does not keep. A table no wider than one block is not cut.

keep

The columns every block repeats, such as the row headings; by default the table's row titles (column 1 unless plan_columns() says otherwise).

col_header

The header each block carries, written once for the whole table in its coordinates and sliced to each block, paginate_cols()'s col_header. NULL slices the header the table has.

fit

TRUE puts every block's widths on page 1's scale (the default: page 1 fills the sheet and a ratio is the same width throughout); FALSE keeps each column's own width.

allow_span_break

TRUE (default) allows a cut inside a spanning header cell.

order

The order the pages come out in, as the axes of the split, outermost first (paginate_cols(order = )): any of "group", "rows" and "cols", or the shorthands "across" and "down". Axes left out follow in that default order.

Value

The plan, with one more layer.

See also

plan_verbs for every verb; paginate_cols() for the split in full.

Other plan verbs: plan_after(), plan_append(), plan_blanks(), plan_cell_style(), plan_cells(), plan_col_header(), plan_columns(), plan_compare(), plan_digits(), plan_empty(), plan_filter(), plan_footnotes(), plan_hide(), plan_labels(), plan_levels(), plan_listing(), plan_nest(), plan_paginate_group(), plan_paginate_rows(), plan_row_group(), plan_sort(), plan_stat_groups(), plan_stub(), plan_style(), plan_titles(), plan_total()

Examples

# Invented laboratory means at five visits: too wide for one page
wide <- data.frame(
  Parameter = c("ALT (U/L)", "AST (U/L)"),
  Day1  = c("22.1", "25.4"), Day8  = c("23.0", "24.8"),
  Day15 = c("30.2", "29.1"), Day22 = c("28.4", "27.0"),
  Day29 = c("26.3", "26.1"))

# Minimal: two visits a page, the parameter repeated on each
pages <- table_plan(wide) |>
  plan_paginate_cols(every = 2, keep = "Parameter") |>
  plan_apply()
length(pages)
#> [1] 3
lapply(pages, function(pg) names(pg$data))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "Parameter" "Day1"      "Day8"     
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "Parameter" "Day15"     "Day22"    
#> 
#> [[3]]
#> [1] "Parameter" "Day29"    
#> 

# The first two weeks on one page and the rest on the next, each column
# keeping its width
pages <- table_plan(wide) |>
  plan_paginate_cols(at = "Day15", keep = "Parameter", fit = FALSE) |>
  plan_apply()
lapply(pages, function(pg) names(pg$data))
#> [[1]]
#> [1] "Parameter" "Day1"      "Day8"     
#> 
#> [[2]]
#> [1] "Parameter" "Day15"     "Day22"     "Day29"    
#> 
pages[[2]]
#> ──────────────────────────────
#> Parameter  Day15  Day22  Day29
#> ──────────────────────────────
#> ALT (U/L)  30.2   28.4   26.3 
#> AST (U/L)  29.1   27.0   26.1 
#> 
#> <rtftable> 2 rows x 4 columns
#>   Row title:  col 1
#>   Borders:    set
#>   Widths:     relative 16.5:20.7:20.7:20.7
#>
